title: Learning Standard Routines, in Three Steps to Perfection
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: In the second installment of his 'NewPDP' product-development framework (building on an earlier 'Drum Beat System' piece), the author argues that most organizations get project planning backward by fixing content first and deriving time and cost from it, producing a bespoke, error-prone plan every single time. His alternative -- fixing time and cost first and applying a standardized, repeatedly-improved template to fit -- is illustrated with his own experience discovering that a 48-month vehicle development timeline admits exactly one workable sequence of non-negotiable activities, which can therefore be written down once and reused, refined by lessons learned each cycle rather than reinvented. The piece structures this into three levels: reusable project templates that specify only what a team needs to independently hit the timeline (explicitly modeled on Prussian military theorist Helmuth von Moltke's mission-order doctrine), standardized processes extracted from those templates whenever a task is both repeated and stable, and dedicated expert groups assigned permanently to those standardized processes so that repetition builds genuine mastery. A pointed section argues that headcount cuts to expert groups don't eliminate the underlying work, only make its cost invisible -- it resurfaces as scattered, unbudgeted extra hours spent by less-experienced staff reinventing what a specialist used to handle instantly. The essay closes by arguing that AI cannot itself create the discipline of standardization; rather, standardized, well-documented processes are the precondition an AI agent needs before it can be handed the work at all, making 'standard first, automation second' the operative sequence.
points: The core inversion -- fix time and cost first, then select content to match, rather than the conventional 'define scope, then derive time and cost' -- is argued to convert every project from a bespoke, error-prone one-off into a repeatable, continuously improvable template.

The von Moltke mission-order principle ('an order should contain everything a subordinate needs to know to independently achieve an objective, and nothing more') is explicitly imported to define what a good template looks like: a skeleton structure, not an exhaustive, over-specified master plan.

The essay identifies a specific accounting illusion in headcount-cutting: eliminating an expert group doesn't eliminate the work, it disperses it invisibly as extra hours across many less-experienced people, so the apparent savings never accounts for the hidden cost that never appears in any budget line.

'Standard first, automation second' reframes AI adoption sequencing: an AI agent can only reliably execute a process that is already documented as a stable, always-the-same standard, so organizations that try to automate work that was never standardized are, in the author's words, 'automating chaos.'
quotes: To develop a completely new vehicle in 48 months, there is exactly one possible approach. I combined the hard, non-negotiable durations of activities that cannot be shortened with sensible durations for the flexible activities.

And what would happen if that didn't produce a new scenario every time, but standardized templates that get applied again and again and deliberately improved through lessons learned? The probability of error drops with every cycle. Delivery reliability rises with every cycle.

It comes from Helmuth von Moltke: "An order should contain everything a subordinate needs to know in order to independently achieve an objective, and nothing more." A template, then, is not a finished plan.
Costs appear to have gone down. The extra effort shows up nowhere. It's spread in hours and half days across hundreds of people, and it never appears in any budget.
AI doesn't help the learning standard routines. The learning standard routines create the precondition for AI to take something like this over entirely, one day.
Standard first, automation second. Whoever tries it the other way around ends up automating chaos.
